newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surplus jumps but U.S. pressure seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Japan surplus jumps but U.S. pressure seen limited.

text.p: Japan's trade surplus for July recorded another hefty jump in figures released on Monday but the rising trend brought only mild expressions of concern from a top U.S. trade official in Tokyo.

The overall customs-cleared surplus climbed nearly 70 percent to 849.08 billion yen ($7.19 billion), while the surplus with the United States grew 36 percent to 420.55 billion yen ($3.56 billion), the Finance Ministry said.

Deputy U.S. Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang, in Tokyo for talks on financial services deregulation, told Reuters before meeting government officials he had not seen the figures but that Washington was concerned about the surplus's rising trend.
July marked the fourth consecutive month in which the surplus has risen sharply and it is expected to show more large rises over the next couple of months.

Economists said that with Japan's domestic demand still recuperating in reaction to a consumer spending spree ahead of a rise in the sales tax in last April 1, imports would remain weak and manufacturers do what came naturally -- export.
Exports rose 12 percent in July, with cars in particular surging 32 percent. In contrast, overall imports managed only a three percent increase.
But economists also said U.S. pressure was likely to be limited.

"Inevitably Japan's trade surplus will be on the mind of U.S. decision-makers. They don't want to politicise it in a sense because they exploited the success of the results-oriented negotiations so they are playing it low, but in reality it is very much on their minds," said Mineko Sasaki- Smith, chief economist at C.S. First Boston.
Others said that with the U.S. economy going strong, including respectable earnings by carmakers, there was little domestic pressure to be heavyhanded with Tokyo.

"It is not as if imports from Japan are acting as a dampener on economic growth. The United States can afford to be generous," said Teruki Morinaga, an economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan (IBJ).

Although Japan's trade surplus with the United States was expected to maintain a solid expanding trend, economic woes in Asia would shrink the size of increases in the surplus six months down the line, economists said.

Weaker growth in some countries and the rise in the yen against Asian currencies after effective devalutions by Thailand, the Philippines and Indonesia in the past two months would mean lower Japanese exports to the region, they said.
"The Asian currency crisis is likely to become a big factor helping to push down the surplus, though it's difficult to say at this stage to what extent," said IBJ's Morinaga.
